**A shallow copy creates a new top-level object or array, but nested objects inside it are still shared by reference with the original.**

### Ways to make one
- Arrays: `[...arr]`, `arr.slice()`, `Array.from(arr)`, `arr.concat()`.
- Objects: `{ ...obj }`, `Object.assign({}, obj)`.

### What is copied and what is shared
- **Primitive values** at the top level are copied, so changing `copy.name` does not affect the original.
- **Nested objects and arrays** are references to the same memory, so changing `copy.address.city` also changes `original.address.city`.

### When a shallow copy is enough
- The data is flat (only primitives).
- You only change top-level fields.
- You are doing immutable updates and will also copy each nested level you change (`{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, name } }`). This is exactly how React and Redux updates work and is efficient because unchanged branches are shared.

### What spread does not copy
- The prototype (the copy is a plain object, so class methods are lost).
- Non-enumerable properties and getters as getters (they are evaluated into plain values).
- Symbols are copied by spread and `Object.assign`.

### When you need more
Use a **deep copy** (`structuredClone`) when you plan to mutate nested data freely and need the original to stay untouched.

j60.a:
**A deep copy duplicates an object and everything nested inside it, so the copy shares no references with the original and can be changed freely without side effects.**

### The modern way: `structuredClone`
Available in all modern browsers, Node.js 17+, Deno and Bun.
- Handles nested objects and arrays, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, typed arrays, `ArrayBuffer`, `Error`, `Blob` and more.
- Handles **circular references**.
- Does **not** copy functions, DOM nodes or class identity (instances become plain objects). It throws a `DataCloneError` for functions and symbols.

### `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))`
The old trick. It only works for plain JSON data: it turns dates into strings, drops `undefined` and functions, converts `NaN` to `null`, loses `Map`/`Set`, and throws on circular references.

### Library or custom
Lodash's `cloneDeep` handles more cases (including keeping prototypes). A custom recursive clone gives full control, for example to preserve class instances. Writing one is a common interview exercise (see "Deep clone an object").

### When to deep copy
- Before mutating data you do not own (a cached API response, a config object).
- To snapshot state for undo, history or tests.

### When not to
Deep copying large structures is expensive. For UI state updates, copying only the path you change (structural sharing) is faster and keeps unchanged references stable for memoisation.

j61.a:
**`find()` returns the first element that matches (or `undefined`) and stops searching immediately; `filter()` returns a new array of all matching elements (possibly empty) and always checks every element.**

| | `find` | `filter` |
|---|---|---|
| Returns | One element or `undefined` | Array (can be empty) |
| Stops early | Yes, at the first match | No, checks all |
| Use for | Looking up one item by id, name, etc. | Getting every matching item |

### Related methods
- **`findIndex`**: index of the first match, or `-1`.
- **`findLast` / `findLastIndex`** (ES2023): search from the end, handy for "the most recent X".
- **`some`**: just `true`/`false`, stops at the first match.
- **`includes`**: for primitive values (`list.includes("a")`).

### Common mistakes
- Using `filter(...)[0]` to get one item: it works but scans the whole array.
- Forgetting `find` can return `undefined`: use optional chaining (`find(...)?.name`) or handle the "not found" case.
- Checking `if (filter(...))`: an empty array is truthy, so this is always true. Check `.length` or use `some`.

### Lookups in big lists
If you look up by id repeatedly, build a `Map` once (`new Map(items.map(i => [i.id, i]))`) and use `map.get(id)`, which is O(1) instead of O(n) per lookup.

j62.a:
**`slice(start, end)` returns a copy of part of an array without changing it; `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` changes the original array in place by removing and/or inserting items, and returns the removed ones.**

| | `slice` | `splice` |
|---|---|---|
| Mutates original | No | Yes |
| Returns | New array with the selected part | Array of removed items |
| `end` / count | End index (exclusive) | How many items to remove |
| Also on strings | Yes (`"hello".slice(1, 3)`) | No |

### slice details
- Negative indexes count from the end: `arr.slice(-2)` gives the last two items.
- `arr.slice()` with no arguments makes a shallow copy.

### splice details
- Remove: `arr.splice(1, 2)` removes two items starting at index 1.
- Insert: `arr.splice(1, 0, "x")` inserts without removing.
- Replace: `arr.splice(1, 1, "x")` swaps one item.

### Immutable alternative: `toSpliced` (ES2023)
`arr.toSpliced(1, 1, "x")` does what `splice` does but returns a new array and leaves the original alone. This is what you want for React state, where mutating with `splice` would not trigger a re-render.

### Memory trick
s**p**lice = changes in **p**lace.

j63.a:
**`push()` adds items to the end of an array and `unshift()` adds them to the beginning; both mutate the array and return its new length, but `unshift` is slower on large arrays because every existing element must move.**

### The four "stack and queue" methods
| Method | Where | Action | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `push(...items)` | End | Add | New length |
| `pop()` | End | Remove | Removed item |
| `unshift(...items)` | Start | Add | New length |
| `shift()` | Start | Remove | Removed item |

### Performance
- `push` and `pop` are O(1) (amortised): nothing else moves.
- `unshift` and `shift` are O(n): every element is re-indexed. On arrays with thousands of items in a hot loop this adds up. For queues with heavy use, consider a dedicated queue structure (a linked list or a circular buffer), or push and read with an index pointer.

### Return values trip people up
Both return the **new length**, not the array. `const arr2 = arr.push(4)` gives a number.

### Immutable versions
For state updates use spread: `[...list, item]` (append) or `[item, ...list]` (prepend).

### Data structure use
- `push` + `pop` = **stack** (last in, first out), e.g. undo history.
- `push` + `shift` = **queue** (first in, first out), e.g. a task list.

j64.a:
**`includes(value, fromIndex?)` returns `true` if an array (or string) contains the given value and `false` otherwise; it is the readable, modern replacement for `indexOf(value) !== -1`.**

### How it compares values
Arrays use the **SameValueZero** algorithm: like `===`, except that `NaN` equals `NaN`. So `[NaN].includes(NaN)` is `true`, while `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` is `-1`.

### Strings
`"hello world".includes("world")` checks for a substring and is **case-sensitive**. Lower-case both sides for case-insensitive search.

### Objects are compared by reference
`[{ id: 1 }].includes({ id: 1 })` is `false`, because the literal creates a different object. To check by content use `some`: `list.some(item => item.id === 1)`.

### Use cases
- Allow-lists: `["admin", "editor"].includes(user.role)`.
- Replacing long `||` chains: `["png", "jpg", "webp"].includes(ext)`.
- Simple search in strings.

### Performance
`includes` is a linear scan (O(n)). For many lookups against a large list, build a `Set` once and use `set.has(value)`, which is O(1).

### fromIndex
Starts searching at that index; negative values count from the end.

j65.a:
**`indexOf(value, fromIndex?)` returns the first index where a value appears in an array or string, or `-1` if it is not found; `lastIndexOf` searches from the end.**

### How it compares
Arrays use **strict equality (`===`)**. That means:
- Objects are matched only if it is the exact same reference.
- `NaN` is never found, because `NaN !== NaN`.

### When to use it
- When you actually need the **position**: to remove an item with `splice`, insert next to it, or find a substring's start.
- Strings: `"hello".indexOf("l")` is `2`.

### When to use something else
- **Just checking existence**: `includes` reads better and handles `NaN`.
- **Matching by a condition** (objects, partial matches): `findIndex(item => item.id === 3)`.
- **Searching from the end by condition**: `findLastIndex`.

### Common bug
`if (list.indexOf(x))` is wrong: index `0` is falsy (so a match at the start looks like "not found"), and `-1` is truthy. Always compare with `-1`, or use `includes`.

### Removing duplicates
`list.filter((x, i) => list.indexOf(x) === i)` keeps only the first occurrence of each value. It is O(n²), so for large arrays `[...new Set(list)]` is far faster.

j66.a:
**`flat(depth = 1)` returns a new array with nested arrays flattened into it up to the given depth; `flat(Infinity)` flattens completely, and `flatMap` maps and flattens one level in a single step.**

### Behaviour
- Default depth is **1**: only one level of nesting is removed.
- `flat(2)`, `flat(3)`... for deeper levels; `flat(Infinity)` for any depth.
- **Empty slots are removed** from sparse arrays.
- Returns a new array; the original is untouched.
- Only arrays are flattened; other iterables (Sets, strings) stay as single elements.

### flatMap
`arr.flatMap(fn)` is the same as `arr.map(fn).flat()` but more efficient. It is very handy when each item should produce **zero, one or many** results:
- Return `[]` to drop an item (filter and map in one pass).
- Return `[a, b]` to expand one item into several.

### Use cases
- Combining results from several requests: `pages.flatMap(p => p.items)`.
- Expanding nested data like categories and their products.
- Turning a tree of menu items into a flat list (with recursion, or `flat(Infinity)` for plain nested arrays).

### Interview angle
You may be asked to implement flattening without `flat`: recursion with `reduce`, or an iterative version using a stack (see "Flatten a nested array").

j67.a:
**`sort(compareFn?)` sorts an array in place and returns the same array; without a compare function it converts items to strings and sorts them by UTF-16 code units, which gives wrong results for numbers.**

### The default-sort trap
`[10, 9, 1, 100].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 100, 9]` because `"10" < "9"` as strings. Always pass a compare function for numbers.

### Compare functions
`(a, b) => result`:
- negative: `a` comes first
- positive: `b` comes first
- `0`: keep their relative order

Patterns:
- Numbers ascending: `(a, b) => a - b`; descending: `(a, b) => b - a`.
- Strings, human-friendly: `(a, b) => a.localeCompare(b)`, which handles accents and case. Pass options like `{ numeric: true }` to sort "file2" before "file10".
- By several keys: compare the first key, and fall back to the next when it is `0` (`a.last.localeCompare(b.last) || a.age - b.age`).

### Stability
Since ES2019, `sort` is **stable**: items that compare equal keep their original order. That makes multi-pass sorting reliable.

### Mutation
`sort` changes the original array, which causes bugs with React state or shared data. Use **`toSorted(compareFn)`** (ES2023) to get a sorted copy, or `[...arr].sort(...)`.

### Performance
Engines use TimSort, O(n log n). For huge data or heavy compare functions, pre-compute sort keys once.

j68.a:
**`reverse()` reverses the order of an array's elements in place and returns that same array; use `toReversed()` (ES2023) when you need a reversed copy instead.**

### Mutation is the main gotcha
Because `reverse` changes the original, calling it on React state, props, a shared module-level array, or the result of a function you do not own causes subtle bugs. Typical example: reversing a list for display also flips the data used elsewhere.

### Non-mutating options
- `arr.toReversed()`: modern and explicit.
- `[...arr].reverse()`: works everywhere.
- `arr.slice().reverse()`: the older idiom.

### Reversing strings
Strings have no `reverse` method. The common approach is `[...str].reverse().join("")`. Use spread rather than `split("")`, because spread splits by code points and keeps emoji and other astral characters intact. (For complex grapheme clusters such as flags or family emoji, use `Intl.Segmenter`.)

### Iterating backwards without copying
If you only need to loop in reverse, a classic `for (let i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)` avoids creating a new array. `findLast`/`findLastIndex` search from the end directly.

### Return value
`reverse` returns the same array reference (useful for chaining, dangerous if you assumed a copy).

j69.a:
**`every(predicate)` returns `true` if the callback returns a truthy value for every element, and stops at the first element that fails; it returns `true` for an empty array.**

### Typical uses
- Validation: `fields.every(f => f.value.trim() !== "")` to enable a submit button.
- Permission checks: `requiredRoles.every(r => user.roles.includes(r))`.
- Type checks: `values.every(Number.isFinite)`.
- "All selected?" checkbox logic.

### Short-circuiting
It stops as soon as one element fails, so it is efficient even on large arrays when a failure appears early.

### The empty array case
`[].every(anything)` is `true`. This is called **vacuous truth**: there is no element that fails. It is logically correct but can surprise you; for example "all items are paid" is `true` for an empty cart. Add an explicit length check when "empty" should mean "no".

### every vs some
- `every`: all must pass (logical AND).
- `some`: at least one must pass (logical OR).
- `!list.some(x => bad(x))` is the same as `list.every(x => !bad(x))`.

### TypeScript tip
`every` accepts a type predicate, so `values.every((v): v is string => typeof v === "string")` narrows `values` to `string[]` inside the `if`.

j70.a:
**`some(predicate)` returns `true` if the callback returns a truthy value for at least one element, stopping at the first match; it returns `false` for an empty array.**

### Typical uses
- "Is there any error?": `fields.some(f => f.error)`.
- Permission checks where any role is enough: `["admin", "owner"].some(r => user.roles.includes(r))`.
- Checking if a list contains an object matching a condition (where `includes` cannot help, because objects are compared by reference).
- "Has the user changed anything?" by comparing fields.

### Short-circuiting
`some` stops at the first truthy result, which makes it efficient. Use it instead of `filter(...).length > 0`, which walks the whole array and allocates a new one.

### some vs find vs includes
- `some`: you only need **yes or no**, with a condition.
- `find`: you need the **matching item** itself.
- `includes`: you are checking for an exact **primitive value**.

### Empty arrays
`[].some(anything)` is `false`: there is no element that matches.

### Logical relationship with every
`list.some(fn)` is equivalent to `!list.every(x => !fn(x))`.

j71.a:
**A Promise is an object representing a value that will be available later: the eventual success or failure of an asynchronous operation; you attach handlers with `.then`, `.catch` and `.finally`, or wait for it with `await`.**

### Why promises exist
They replaced deeply nested callbacks with a chainable, composable model where errors flow to a single handler, and they are the foundation of `async/await`.

### Creating one
`new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })` runs the executor immediately. Call `resolve(value)` on success or `reject(error)` on failure. In practice you mostly **consume** promises returned by APIs like `fetch` rather than creating them. Shortcuts: `Promise.resolve(value)`, `Promise.reject(error)`, and `Promise.withResolvers()` (ES2024), which returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }` for cases where you resolve from outside.

### Consuming
- `.then(onSuccess)` returns a **new** promise, which enables chaining.
- `.catch(onError)` handles any rejection earlier in the chain.
- `.finally(fn)` runs either way, for cleanup like hiding a spinner.
- `await promise` inside an `async` function.

### Key properties
- A promise settles **once**; later `resolve`/`reject` calls are ignored.
- Handlers always run **asynchronously**, as microtasks, even if the promise is already resolved.
- Unhandled rejections produce warnings (and can crash Node.js), so always handle errors.

### Combinators
`Promise.all`, `allSettled`, `race` and `any` run several promises together.

j72.q: What are the states of a Promise?
j72.a:
**A promise is always in one of three states: pending (not finished yet), fulfilled (finished with a value) or rejected (finished with a reason, usually an `Error`); once it leaves pending it is settled and can never change again.**

### The states
- **Pending**: the initial state. The operation is still running.
- **Fulfilled**: `resolve(value)` was called with a non-promise value. `.then` handlers receive the value.
- **Rejected**: `reject(reason)` was called or the executor threw. `.catch` handlers receive the reason.

"Settled" is the umbrella term for fulfilled or rejected.

### Resolved is not the same as fulfilled
Calling `resolve(anotherPromise)` makes the promise **follow** the other one. It is "resolved" (locked in) but still pending until that other promise settles, and it may end up rejected. That is also why returning a promise from `.then` waits for it.

### Immutability of the outcome
- Only the first `resolve` or `reject` counts; the rest are ignored.
- Handlers added after settlement still run, receiving the stored value.

### Inspecting the state
There is no public `promise.state` property. In tests or debugging you can use `Promise.race` with a sentinel value, or the browser and Node consoles show `<pending>`, `<fulfilled>` or `<rejected>` when you log a promise.

### Why it matters
It explains why a promise can safely be shared and awaited from multiple places: everyone receives the same final result.

j73.a:
**`async`/`await` is syntax for working with promises that reads like synchronous code: an `async` function always returns a promise, and `await` pauses that function until a promise settles, giving you its value or throwing its error.**

### How it works
- `async function f() { return 1; }` returns `Promise<1>`.
- `await somePromise` suspends the function (not the whole program). The rest of the function continues as a microtask once the promise settles.
- A rejected promise makes `await` **throw**, so you handle errors with ordinary `try/catch`.
- `await` works with any "thenable" and with plain values (which are wrapped).

### Where you can use `await`
- Inside `async` functions (including arrow functions and class methods).
- At the **top level of ES modules** (top-level await), e.g. to load config before exporting.

### Sequential vs parallel
A common performance bug is awaiting independent operations one after another:
- **Sequential**: `const a = await getA(); const b = await getB();` takes the sum of both times.
- **Parallel**: `const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]);` takes the time of the slowest.
Await in sequence only when the second call depends on the first.

### Pitfalls
- Forgetting `await` gives you a pending promise instead of the value.
- `forEach(async ...)` does not wait. Use `for...of` or `Promise.all`.
- Errors thrown after an `await` are rejections of the returned promise; the caller must handle them.

j74.q: How to handle errors in async/await?
j74.a:
**Wrap awaited calls in `try/catch` (with `finally` for cleanup); a rejected promise makes `await` throw, so you handle async errors exactly like synchronous ones, and any error you do not catch rejects the async function's own promise.**

### Patterns
- **`try/catch/finally`** around one or more awaits. Use `finally` for cleanup (hide a loading spinner, release a lock).
- **Catch at the right level**: handle errors where you can do something useful (show a message, retry, fall back). Otherwise let them propagate to a central handler.
- **`.catch` on a single call** for a quick fallback: `const data = await load().catch(() => defaultData);`
- **Check `response.ok` with fetch**: `fetch` only rejects on network failure, not on HTTP 404 or 500. Throw yourself when `!response.ok`.
- **`Promise.allSettled`** when several operations run together and you want every result, including failures.
- **Error causes** (ES2022): `throw new Error("Failed to load profile", { cause: err })` adds context without losing the original error.
- **Custom error classes** (`class HttpError extends Error`) so callers can branch with `instanceof`.

### Things that are not caught
- Promises you did not `await` (fire-and-forget). Their rejection escapes the `try`. Either await them or attach `.catch`.
- Errors inside callbacks that run later (e.g. inside `setTimeout`).

### Last line of defence
Browsers fire `unhandledrejection`; Node has `process.on("unhandledRejection")`. Log there, but do not rely on it for normal flow.

j75.a:
**`Promise.all(iterable)` runs promises concurrently and returns a single promise that fulfills with an array of all results (in the original order) once every one succeeds, or rejects immediately with the first error.**

### Behaviour
- **Order is preserved**: results match the input order, not the order they finished.
- **Fail-fast**: as soon as one promise rejects, the combined promise rejects with that reason. The other operations keep running in the background (promises cannot be cancelled), but their results are ignored.
- Non-promise values in the array are treated as already fulfilled.
- An empty array fulfills immediately with `[]`.

### When to use it
When you need **all** results and the operations are independent: loading a page's user, settings and notifications at once; uploading several files; fetching several pages of data.

### Related combinators
- **`Promise.allSettled`**: wait for all and get each outcome, success or failure. Use when partial success is fine.
- **`Promise.race`**: settles with the first promise to settle (success or failure). Good for timeouts.
- **`Promise.any`**: fulfills with the first **success**; rejects with an `AggregateError` only if all fail.

### Watch out for
- **Too much concurrency**: `Promise.all(10_000 requests)` fires everything at once. Batch the work or use a concurrency limit.
- **Cancellation**: pair it with an `AbortController` if you want the other requests to stop when one fails.

j76.a:
**`Promise.race(iterable)` returns a promise that settles the same way as the first input promise to settle, whether that first one fulfills or rejects.**

### Typical uses
- **Timeouts**: race the real operation against a promise that rejects after N milliseconds.
- **Fastest source wins**: query a cache and the network and use whichever answers first (though `Promise.any` is usually better here, because it ignores failures).
- **Cancellation signals**: race work against a promise that rejects when the user navigates away.

### race vs any
- `race`: the first to **settle** wins, even if it is a failure.
- `any`: the first to **succeed** wins; it rejects only if every promise fails (with an `AggregateError`).

### Important caveats
- **The losers keep running.** A timed-out `fetch` still completes in the background and still uses bandwidth. To actually stop it, use an `AbortController` (`fetch(url, { signal })`). For simple timeouts, `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` does both in one step.
- An **empty** iterable gives a promise that stays pending forever.
- Clear your timeout timer when the real operation wins, or it keeps the process (or test runner) alive.

### Modern timeout pattern
`fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })` rejects with a `TimeoutError` and cancels the request, which is cleaner than a race for fetch specifically. `Promise.race` remains the general tool for any promise.

j77.a:
**`Promise.allSettled(iterable)` waits for every promise to finish, whether it succeeds or fails, and fulfills with an array of result objects describing each outcome; it never rejects.**

### Result shape
Each item is either:
- `{ status: "fulfilled", value }`
- `{ status: "rejected", reason }`

Results are in the same order as the input.

### When to use it
When operations are **independent** and partial success is acceptable:
- Loading several dashboard widgets: show the ones that worked and an error card for the rest.
- Sending notifications to many recipients and reporting which failed.
- Cleanup tasks where every one should be attempted.
- Batch uploads with a per-file status.

### allSettled vs all
- `Promise.all` is **all-or-nothing** and rejects on the first failure, losing the other results.
- `Promise.allSettled` **always** gives you every outcome.

### Handling the results
Split them with `filter` on `status`, or use `Object.groupBy(results, r => r.status)`. Remember that `allSettled` itself never rejects, so a `try/catch` around it will not catch the individual failures. You must inspect each result.

### Retrying failures
A common pattern is to run `allSettled`, collect the rejected items, and retry just those.

j78.a:
**The Fetch API is the built-in, promise-based way to make HTTP requests in browsers, Node.js (18+), Deno, Bun and edge runtimes: `fetch(url, options)` returns a promise of a `Response`.**

### Basic flow
1. `const res = await fetch(url, options)`.
2. Check `res.ok` (status 200-299) or `res.status`.
3. Read the body once with `res.json()`, `res.text()`, `res.blob()`, `res.arrayBuffer()` or `res.formData()`.

### The surprise: HTTP errors do not reject
`fetch` rejects **only** on network failures (offline, DNS, CORS blocked, aborted). A 404 or 500 **fulfills** normally. Always check `res.ok` and throw yourself.

### Common options
- `method`: `"POST"`, `"PUT"`, `"DELETE"`...
- `headers`: e.g. `{ "Content-Type": "application/json", Authorization: "Bearer ..." }`
- `body`: a string (`JSON.stringify(data)`), `FormData`, `Blob` or `URLSearchParams`. With `FormData`, do not set `Content-Type` yourself; the browser adds the multipart boundary.
- `signal`: an `AbortSignal` to cancel, e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`.
- `credentials`: `"include"` to send cookies cross-origin.
- `cache`: control the HTTP cache. In Next.js, `fetch` also accepts `next: { revalidate, tags }`.

### Good habits
- Wrap fetch in a small helper that checks `ok`, parses JSON and throws a meaningful error.
- Cancel requests that are no longer needed (component unmount, a new search) with `AbortController`.
- A body can be read only once; use `res.clone()` if you need it twice.

j79.a:
**Axios is a popular third-party HTTP client library with a promise-based API that adds conveniences on top of the platform's request functions, such as automatic JSON handling, interceptors, rejecting on HTTP errors and instance-wide defaults.**

### What it adds compared to `fetch`
- **Rejects on HTTP errors** (4xx/5xx) by default, so a failed request goes straight to `catch`.
- **Automatic JSON**: request bodies are serialised and responses parsed (`response.data`).
- **Interceptors**: run code before every request (attach auth tokens) or after every response (refresh tokens, central error logging).
- **Instances**: `axios.create({ baseURL, timeout, headers })` for each API.
- **Timeouts** via a simple option, and upload/download progress events.
- Works the same in the browser and Node.

### fetch today
Native `fetch` is now available everywhere (browsers, Node 18+, Deno, Bun, edge runtimes) and supports `AbortSignal.timeout`, streaming and the Next.js caching extensions. Many teams now write a 20-line `fetch` wrapper instead of adding a dependency. Axios still makes sense when you want interceptors and its conventions across a large codebase.

### Things to know
- Axios errors carry `error.response` (server replied with an error status), `error.request` (no response) or neither (setup error).
- Cancel requests with an `AbortController` signal (the old `CancelToken` is deprecated).
- In Next.js, prefer `fetch` in Server Components so you get built-in caching and revalidation.

j80.a:
**An API call is a request your code sends to another program's interface (usually a web server over HTTP) to read or change data, followed by a response, typically in JSON.**

### Anatomy of an HTTP API call
- **URL / endpoint**: `https://api.example.com/users/42`
- **Method**: `GET` (read), `POST` (create), `PUT`/`PATCH` (update), `DELETE` (remove).
- **Headers**: metadata such as `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `Accept`.
- **Body**: data sent with `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`, usually JSON.
- **Response**: a status code (`200` OK, `201` Created, `400` Bad Request, `401` Unauthorized, `404` Not Found, `500` Server Error), headers, and a body.

### Making a call in JavaScript
With `fetch` (built in) or a library like Axios. The call is asynchronous, so you use `await` or `.then`.

### What a robust API call handles
- **Loading state** while waiting.
- **Errors**: network failures and HTTP error statuses (remember `fetch` does not reject on 4xx/5xx).
- **Timeouts and cancellation** with `AbortController`.
- **Validation** of the response shape before using it.
- **Retries** with backoff for temporary failures (and only for idempotent requests).
- **Security**: never put secret API keys in browser code; call your own backend, which holds the secrets.

### Types of APIs
REST (resource URLs), GraphQL (one endpoint, query language), RPC-style (including Next.js Server Actions), WebSockets for real-time, and browser APIs (Geolocation, Clipboard) that are "APIs" in the broader sense.

j81.a:
**The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live, tree-shaped object representation of an HTML document; JavaScript reads and changes the page through it, and the browser re-renders whatever changes.**

### The tree
The browser parses HTML into **nodes**: the `document` at the root, then element nodes (`<html>`, `<body>`, `<div>`), text nodes, comment nodes and attributes. Each element node is an object with properties (`id`, `className`, `value`), methods (`append`, `remove`, `addEventListener`) and relationships (`parentElement`, `children`, `nextElementSibling`).

### DOM vs HTML source
The DOM is not the HTML file. The browser fixes invalid markup, adds missing tags (like `<tbody>`), and JavaScript changes the DOM after load. DevTools' Elements panel shows the **current DOM**, while "View Source" shows the original HTML.

### What you do with it
- Find elements: `querySelector`, `querySelectorAll`, `getElementById`.
- Change content and structure: `textContent`, `append`, `remove`, `replaceWith`.
- Change appearance: `classList`, `style`.
- React to users: `addEventListener`.

### Performance
Reading layout properties (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect`) after writes forces the browser to recalculate layout. Batch reads and writes, and build many nodes off-screen (e.g. in a `DocumentFragment`) before inserting them.

### Frameworks
React, Vue, Svelte and Angular manage the DOM for you and update only what changed; you rarely touch it directly, but knowing it explains what they do under the hood.

j82.a:
**DOM manipulation means using JavaScript to create, change, move or remove elements, attributes, text and styles on the page after it has loaded.**

### Core operations
- **Create**: `document.createElement("li")`, `document.createTextNode(text)`, or `<template>` cloning.
- **Insert**: `parent.append(...nodes)`, `prepend`, `before`, `after`, `replaceWith`, `insertAdjacentHTML/Element`.
- **Remove**: `element.remove()`.
- **Content**: `textContent` (safe for text) or `innerHTML` (parses HTML, an XSS risk with user input).
- **Attributes**: `setAttribute`, `getAttribute`, `removeAttribute`, `toggleAttribute`, and `dataset` for `data-*` attributes.
- **Classes and styles**: `classList.add/remove/toggle`, `element.style.setProperty`.

### Doing it efficiently
- **Batch DOM writes**: build many nodes in a `DocumentFragment` (or an array passed to one `append`) and insert once.
- **Avoid layout thrashing**: do not alternate reading layout (`offsetHeight`) and writing styles in a loop.
- **Prefer classes over inline styles** so CSS controls appearance.
- **Use event delegation** instead of a listener per item.
- **Animate with CSS transforms/opacity**, not layout properties.

### Safety
Never insert untrusted strings with `innerHTML`. Use `textContent`, or sanitise with a library like DOMPurify, or the newer `setHTML` Sanitizer API where supported.

### Frameworks vs manual
Frameworks are better for complex, state-driven UIs. Direct manipulation is still right for small widgets, progressive enhancement and performance-critical spots.

j83.a:
**Event bubbling is the phase where an event, after reaching its target element, travels back up through each ancestor (parent, grandparent, up to `document` and `window`), triggering their listeners for the same event.**

### The full journey of an event
1. **Capturing phase**: from `window` down to the target's parent.
2. **Target phase**: on the element that was actually clicked.
3. **Bubbling phase**: back up from the target to `window`.

Listeners added normally (`addEventListener(type, fn)`) run in the bubbling phase.

### target vs currentTarget
- `event.target`: the element where the event started (the innermost clicked element).
- `event.currentTarget`: the element whose listener is running right now.

### Stopping it
- `event.stopPropagation()`: stops the event from reaching further ancestors.
- `event.stopImmediatePropagation()`: also stops other listeners on the same element.
Use these sparingly; they can break analytics, outside-click handlers for dropdowns, and delegated listeners elsewhere.

### Not every event bubbles
`focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter`, `mouseleave`, `load` and `scroll` (on elements) do not bubble. Bubbling alternatives exist: `focusin`/`focusout`, `mouseover`/`mouseout`. Check `event.bubbles`.

### Why it is useful
Bubbling makes **event delegation** possible: one listener on a parent handles events for all its children, including ones added later.

j84.a:
**Event capturing is the first phase of event propagation, where the event travels from `window` down through each ancestor towards the target; you listen during it by passing `{ capture: true }` (or `true`) to `addEventListener`.**

### Propagation order
1. **Capture**: `window` → `document` → `html` → `body` → ... → parent of target.
2. **Target**: listeners on the target itself.
3. **Bubble**: back up from the target to `window`.

So a capturing listener on an ancestor runs **before** any listener on the target, and a bubbling listener on the same ancestor runs **after**.

### When capturing is useful
- **Intercepting events first**: e.g. a global handler that blocks clicks while a modal is open, or logs every interaction before components see it.
- **Handling non-bubbling events at a parent**: `focus`, `blur`, `load` and `scroll` do not bubble, but they do go through the capture phase. `form.addEventListener("focus", fn, true)` sees focus on every input.
- **Outside-click detection** that should run before inner components stop propagation.

### Removing a capturing listener
The capture flag is part of the listener's identity: `removeEventListener(type, fn, true)` must pass `true` again, or nothing is removed.

### In React
React supports capture-phase handlers with the `Capture` suffix: `onClickCapture`, `onFocusCapture`.

j85.a:
**Event delegation is attaching one event listener to a common ancestor instead of to each child, and using `event.target` (usually with `closest()`) to work out which child the event came from; it relies on events bubbling up.**

### Why use it
- **Fewer listeners**: one listener for a list of 1,000 items instead of 1,000.
- **Dynamic content just works**: items added later are handled automatically, with no need to attach new listeners.
- **Less cleanup**: nothing to remove when items are deleted, which also avoids leaks.

### How to do it well
1. Listen on a stable parent (the list, table or container).
2. In the handler, find the relevant element with `event.target.closest(selector)`. This handles clicks on nested elements, like an icon inside a button.
3. Check that the found element is inside your container (`container.contains(el)`).
4. Read what to do from `data-*` attributes (`data-action="delete"`, `data-id="42"`).

### Limitations
- Only works for events that bubble (use `focusin`/`focusout` instead of `focus`/`blur`).
- If a child calls `stopPropagation()`, the parent never sees the event.
- Very frequent events (`mousemove`) on huge containers can do more work per event than targeted listeners.

### Frameworks
React attaches listeners at the root of the app and dispatches to components, which is delegation done for you.

j86.a:
**`target.addEventListener(type, listener, options)` registers a function to run when an event of that type happens on a DOM element, `document`, `window` or any other `EventTarget`; you can add many listeners for the same event.**

### Options
- **`once: true`**: run the listener a single time, then remove it automatically.
- **`passive: true`**: promise not to call `preventDefault()`. Browsers can then scroll immediately, which makes `touchstart`, `touchmove` and `wheel` listeners smoother.
- **`capture: true`**: listen in the capture phase instead of the bubble phase.
- **`signal`**: an `AbortSignal`; calling `controller.abort()` removes every listener registered with it. This is the cleanest way to clean up many listeners at once (for example when a component unmounts).

### Removing listeners
`removeEventListener(type, sameFunction, sameCaptureFlag)` needs the **exact same function reference**, so inline arrow functions cannot be removed. Keep a reference, or use `signal`.

### Compared to `onclick`
`element.onclick = fn` holds only one handler; assigning again replaces it. `addEventListener` supports multiple handlers and the options above.

### Inside the listener
- `event.target` (origin) vs `event.currentTarget` (the element the listener is on).
- `event.preventDefault()` stops default behaviour (form submit, link navigation).
- With a normal function, `this` is `currentTarget`; with an arrow function, use `event.currentTarget`.

### Custom events
`target.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("cart:add", { detail: {...} }))` lets parts of your app communicate through the DOM.

j87.a: **`textContent` reads or sets an element's plain text (safe, fast, no HTML parsing); `innerHTML` reads or sets its HTML markup, which the browser parses into elements, so it is powerful but dangerous with untrusted input.** ### textContent - **Setting** replaces all children with a single text node. Characters like `<` are shown literally, never interpreted. - **Reading** returns the text of all descendants, including text hidden with CSS and inside `

j88.a:
**`querySelector(selector)` returns the first element matching a CSS selector (or `null`), and `querySelectorAll(selector)` returns a static `NodeList` of all matches; both work on `document` or on any element to search inside it.**

### Selectors you can use
Anything CSS supports: `#id`, `.class`, `tag`, attributes (`[data-id="3"]`, `input[type=email]`), combinators (`.card > h2`, `ul li`), pseudo-classes (`:checked`, `:not(.hidden)`, `li:nth-child(2n)`, `:has(img)`).

### Scoping
`container.querySelector(".title")` searches only inside `container`, which is faster and avoids matching elements elsewhere on the page.

### Static vs live collections
- `querySelectorAll` returns a **static** snapshot: adding elements later does not change it.
- `getElementsByClassName` / `getElementsByTagName` return **live** `HTMLCollection`s that update automatically, which can surprise you inside loops.

### Working with the results
- `NodeList` supports `forEach` and `for...of`, but not `map`/`filter`. Convert with `[...nodeList]` or `Array.from(nodeList)`.
- Always handle `null` from `querySelector`: `document.querySelector("#missing")?.remove()`.

### Related methods
- `element.closest(selector)`: walks **up** to the nearest matching ancestor (great for event delegation).
- `element.matches(selector)`: checks whether an element matches.
- `getElementById` is slightly faster for a single id, but the difference rarely matters.

### Escaping
For ids or values with special characters, use `CSS.escape(value)` inside the selector.

j89.a:
**`element.classList` is a live list of an element's CSS classes with methods to add, remove, toggle, replace and check classes, which is far safer than editing the `className` string by hand.**

### Methods
- `add("a", "b")`: adds one or more classes (no duplicates).
- `remove("a", "b")`: removes classes (no error if missing).
- `toggle("open")`: adds if missing, removes if present; returns the new state.
- `toggle("open", condition)`: forces add (`true`) or remove (`false`). Ideal for syncing a class with state.
- `contains("open")`: checks for a class.
- `replace("old", "new")`: swaps one class for another.
- It is iterable, and `length`/`item(i)` work too.

### Why prefer it over className
`element.className = "active"` overwrites every other class. Concatenating strings leads to duplicates and spacing bugs. `classList` changes only what you ask.

### Good practice
- Toggle classes and let CSS handle appearance and transitions, instead of setting many inline styles.
- Keep state classes clearly named (`is-open`, `is-loading`, `has-error`).
- For accessibility, pair visual classes with ARIA attributes (`aria-expanded`, `aria-hidden`), because screen readers do not see classes.

### SVG
`classList` works on SVG elements too, where `className` is an object rather than a string.

j90.a:
**`element.dataset` gives read/write access to an element's custom `data-*` attributes as a plain object, converting names from kebab-case in HTML (`data-user-id`) to camelCase in JavaScript (`dataset.userId`).**

### Rules
- `data-user-id="42"` ↔ `element.dataset.userId === "42"`.
- Values are **always strings**. Convert them yourself: `Number(el.dataset.id)`, `el.dataset.active === "true"`, or `JSON.parse` for small JSON.
- Setting `el.dataset.status = "done"` adds `data-status="done"` to the HTML.
- `delete el.dataset.status` removes the attribute.
- `"status" in el.dataset` checks for it.

### Common uses
- **Event delegation**: store an id and action on the element (`data-id`, `data-action`) and read them in one parent listener.
- **Configuration for widgets**: `<div data-carousel data-interval="5000">`.
- **CSS hooks**: style with attribute selectors (`[data-state="open"]`), which pairs nicely with state-driven UI. Libraries like Radix UI expose `data-state` for exactly this.
- Passing server-rendered values to client scripts.

### What not to store
- Sensitive data: it is visible in the HTML to anyone.
- Large or complex data: keep that in JavaScript (a `Map` keyed by id).
- Anything that duplicates state you already hold elsewhere and may go out of sync.

j91.a:
**Both store string key-value pairs in the browser with the same API, but `localStorage` persists until it is cleared (across tabs and restarts), while `sessionStorage` lasts only for one tab's session and is deleted when that tab closes.**

| | `localStorage` | `sessionStorage` |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | Until cleared by code, the user or the browser | Until the tab/window closes |
| Shared between tabs (same origin) | Yes | No, each tab has its own |
| Survives reload | Yes | Yes |
| Capacity | About 5 MB per origin | About 5 MB per origin |
| `storage` event in other tabs | Yes | No |

### API (identical)
`setItem(key, value)`, `getItem(key)` (returns `null` if missing), `removeItem(key)`, `clear()`, `key(index)`, `length`.

### Important details
- **Strings only**: store objects with `JSON.stringify` and read them with a guarded `JSON.parse`.
- **Synchronous**: it blocks the main thread; fine for small data, bad for large or frequent writes.
- **Can throw**: in private browsing modes, when storage is disabled, or when the quota is full. Wrap access in `try/catch`.
- **Not secure**: any JavaScript on the page (including an XSS payload) can read it. Never store auth tokens or secrets there; prefer HttpOnly cookies for sessions.
- **Not available on the server** (SSR), so read it inside effects or event handlers.

### Choosing
- `localStorage`: preferences, drafts, cached non-sensitive data.
- `sessionStorage`: per-tab state like a multi-step form or a scroll position.
- Larger or structured data: **IndexedDB**.

j92.a:
**Cookies are small pieces of data (about 4 KB each) that a server or script stores in the browser and that the browser automatically sends back with every matching HTTP request; they are mainly used for sessions, preferences and tracking.**

### Setting cookies
- **Server**: `Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=3600`.
- **JavaScript**: `document.cookie = "theme=dark; Max-Age=31536000; Path=/; SameSite=Lax"`. Each assignment sets one cookie; reading `document.cookie` returns all readable cookies as one string.
- A newer async API, **`cookieStore`**, is available in Chromium-based browsers.

### Attributes that matter
- **`HttpOnly`**: JavaScript cannot read it. Essential for session cookies, so an XSS attack cannot steal them.
- **`Secure`**: sent only over HTTPS.
- **`SameSite`**: `Lax` (default in modern browsers: sent on top-level navigations, not on cross-site sub-requests), `Strict` (never cross-site), `None` (always, requires `Secure`). This is the main defence against CSRF.
- **`Max-Age` / `Expires`**: without them it is a session cookie, removed when the browser closes.
- **`Domain` / `Path`**: which requests receive it.
- **`Partitioned`** (CHIPS): third-party cookies kept separate per top-level site.

### Cookies vs Web Storage
Cookies travel with **every** request (adding bytes to each one), are small, and can be HttpOnly. `localStorage` stays in the browser, is bigger, and is always readable by JavaScript.

### Privacy changes
Browsers increasingly restrict **third-party cookies** used for cross-site tracking, and privacy laws (GDPR) require consent for non-essential cookies.

j93.a:
**Web APIs are the interfaces the browser (or another host) provides to JavaScript beyond the core language, such as the DOM, `fetch`, timers, storage, Canvas, geolocation, the clipboard, Web Workers and many more.**

### Language vs platform
ECMAScript defines the language (syntax, types, `Promise`, `Array`). Everything that touches the outside world comes from the host. The browser exposes Web APIs through `window` (and `self` in workers); Node.js exposes its own APIs (and now implements many web standards like `fetch`, `URL`, `AbortController` and Web Streams).

### Well-known groups
- **Document and UI**: DOM, events, `IntersectionObserver`, `ResizeObserver`, `MutationObserver`, View Transitions, Popover.
- **Network**: `fetch`, WebSocket, Server-Sent Events (`EventSource`), WebRTC.
- **Storage**: `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, IndexedDB, Cache API, cookies, the Origin Private File System.
- **Concurrency and timing**: `setTimeout`, `requestAnimationFrame`, `requestIdleCallback`, Web Workers, `BroadcastChannel`.
- **Device and media**: Geolocation, Clipboard, Notifications, MediaDevices (camera and microphone), Web Audio, Vibration.
- **Graphics**: Canvas, WebGL, WebGPU.
- **Offline and installability**: Service Workers, Web App Manifest, Push.

### How they work with the event loop
Many Web APIs run outside the JavaScript thread (network, timers, workers) and deliver results back through the task or microtask queue.

### Feature detection and permissions
Check support before use (`if ("geolocation" in navigator)`), and expect permission prompts for sensitive APIs, many of which also require HTTPS ("secure contexts").

j94.a:
**`setTimeout(fn, delay)` runs a function once after at least `delay` milliseconds; `setInterval(fn, delay)` runs it repeatedly every `delay` milliseconds until you stop it with `clearInterval`.**

### Both
- Return an id you pass to `clearTimeout` / `clearInterval`.
- Accept extra arguments that are passed to the callback.
- Are **minimum** delays, not guarantees. The callback runs only when the call stack is empty and the event loop reaches it, so busy code delays it.
- Are throttled in background tabs (often to once per second or less) and nested timers are clamped to at least 4 ms after a few levels.

### Problems with setInterval
- It schedules the next run regardless of whether the previous one finished. If the callback is slow or async (a network poll), runs can overlap or pile up.
- It keeps going forever if you forget to clear it, which is a common memory leak in components.

### Recursive setTimeout
Scheduling the next run at the end of the current one guarantees a gap between runs and makes it easy to change the delay (backoff) or stop based on a condition. This is the preferred pattern for polling.

### For animations
Use `requestAnimationFrame`, which syncs with the display refresh rate and pauses in hidden tabs.

### Cleanup
In React, clear timers in the effect cleanup function so they do not fire after the component unmounts.

j95.a:
**`clearTimeout(id)` cancels a timer created by `setTimeout` before it fires, using the id that `setTimeout` returned; calling it with an id that already fired or is invalid does nothing.**

### Where it is essential
- **Debounce**: every new call clears the previous timer and starts a new one.
- **Component cleanup**: clear pending timers when a component unmounts (in a React effect's cleanup), otherwise the callback may update state that no longer exists.
- **Cancelling delayed actions**: "undo send" within 5 seconds, hiding a tooltip unless the pointer leaves, auto-logout warnings.
- **Timeouts for async work**: clear the timeout when the real operation finishes first.

### Details
- In browsers the id is a positive integer. In Node it is a `Timeout` object (which also has `ref()`/`unref()`).
- `clearTimeout` and `clearInterval` are technically interchangeable in browsers, but use the matching one for clarity.
- Keep the id in a variable that outlives the scheduling call (a closure, a ref, or an object property).

### Common bug
Storing the timer id in a variable that is recreated on every render (a plain variable in a React function component). The cleanup then clears the wrong id. Use the effect cleanup or a `useRef`.

j96.a:
**The History API (`window.history`) lets JavaScript move through the browser's session history and change the URL without reloading the page, using `pushState`, `replaceState` and the `popstate` event; it is the foundation of client-side routing.**

### Methods
- **`history.pushState(state, "", url)`**: adds a new entry and changes the address bar. No request is made and no `popstate` fires.
- **`history.replaceState(state, "", url)`**: changes the current entry instead of adding one, useful for updating query params (filters, search) without growing the back stack.
- **`history.back()`, `forward()`, `go(n)`**: navigate like the browser buttons.
- **`history.state`**: the state object of the current entry.
- **`history.length`**: number of entries in this tab's session.

### The popstate event
Fires when the user navigates with back/forward (or you call `back`/`go`). Your router reads `location` and `event.state` and renders the matching view.

### Rules
- URLs must be **same-origin**.
- The `state` object must be structured-cloneable and is limited in size.
- After `pushState`, the server must be able to handle that URL on a refresh (serve the app shell for all routes).

### Navigation API
A newer API, `window.navigation`, gives a single `navigate` event for all navigations (links, forms, back/forward) and is supported in Chromium browsers and recent Safari and Firefox releases.

### In frameworks
React Router, Next.js and others wrap this. In Next.js, `window.history.pushState/replaceState` also integrate with the router.

j97.a:
**`window.location` represents the current page's URL: you can read its parts (protocol, host, path, query, hash) and change it to navigate, reload or redirect.**

### Reading the URL
- `location.href`: the full URL.
- `location.origin`: protocol + host + port.
- `location.pathname`: `/products/42`.
- `location.search`: `?sort=price&page=2`. Parse it with **`URLSearchParams`**.
- `location.hash`: `#reviews`.
- `location.host`, `hostname`, `port`, `protocol`.

### Navigating
- `location.assign(url)` or `location.href = url`: navigate and **add** a history entry.
- `location.replace(url)`: navigate and **replace** the current entry, so Back does not return to it. Use it for redirects such as after login.
- `location.reload()`: reload the page.
- Setting `location.hash` jumps to an anchor without reloading and fires `hashchange`.

### Location vs History API
Changing `location` (except the hash) loads a new page. The History API changes the URL **without** loading anything, for single-page apps.

### Working with URLs
The `URL` class parses and builds URLs safely: `new URL(path, location.origin)`, `url.searchParams.set("page", "2")`. Avoid concatenating query strings by hand; `URLSearchParams` handles encoding.

### Security
Never redirect to a URL taken directly from user input or a query parameter (`?next=...`) without validating it: open redirects are used in phishing. Allow only same-origin or known destinations.

j98.a:
**`window.navigator` describes the browser and device the page is running on and is the entry point to many device-related APIs, such as clipboard, geolocation, online status, language, service workers and media devices.**

### Useful properties
- `navigator.onLine`: whether the browser believes it has a network connection (listen to `online`/`offline` events for changes).
- `navigator.language` / `languages`: the user's preferred languages, useful for i18n defaults.
- `navigator.hardwareConcurrency`: number of logical CPU cores, useful for sizing worker pools.
- `navigator.userAgent`: the user-agent string. It is unreliable and being reduced for privacy; prefer feature detection or `navigator.userAgentData` where supported.
- `navigator.cookieEnabled`, `navigator.maxTouchPoints`.

### APIs hanging off navigator
- `navigator.clipboard`: read/write the clipboard (requires a user gesture and HTTPS).
- `navigator.geolocation`: location, with a permission prompt.
- `navigator.serviceWorker`: register service workers for offline support and push.
- `navigator.mediaDevices`: camera and microphone (`getUserMedia`), screen capture.
- `navigator.share`: the native share sheet on supporting devices.
- `navigator.sendBeacon(url, data)`: reliably send analytics when the page is closing.
- `navigator.storage`: storage estimates and `persist()`.
- `navigator.permissions.query`: check permission state without prompting.

### Feature detection
Always check that an API exists before using it (`if ("share" in navigator)`), and handle rejections, since users can deny permissions.

j99.a:
**CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that lets a server explicitly allow web pages from other origins to read its responses, using HTTP headers like `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`; without that permission, the browser blocks the page's JavaScript from reading the response.**

### Why it exists
The **same-origin policy** stops a page on `a.com` from reading data from `b.com` with the user's cookies. CORS is the controlled exception: the server at `b.com` says which origins may read its responses.

### Simple vs preflighted requests
- **Simple requests** (`GET`/`HEAD`/`POST` with basic headers and content types like form data): the browser sends the request with an `Origin` header and checks the response's `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
- **Preflighted requests** (other methods like `PUT`/`DELETE`, custom headers such as `Authorization`, or `Content-Type: application/json`): the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` request asking permission. The server must reply with `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` (cacheable with `Access-Control-Max-Age`).

### Credentials
To send cookies cross-origin, the client uses `credentials: "include"`, and the server must reply with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` **and a specific origin**, not `*`.

### Key facts for interviews
- CORS is enforced **by the browser**. Servers, `curl` and Postman ignore it.
- A CORS error means the **request may still have reached the server**; only reading the response was blocked. It is not a protection against CSRF.
- It is fixed on the **server** (or with a proxy on your own origin), never in client code.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is fine for public data, never for authenticated APIs.

j100.a: **The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) is the browser's core security rule that a page can freely interact only with resources from the same origin (same scheme, host and port); reading data from other origins is blocked unless they opt in, for example with CORS.** ### What counts as the same origin Scheme + host + port must all match. - `https://app.example.com` vs `https://app.example.com/page`: same origin. - vs `http://app.example.com`: different scheme. - vs `https://api.example.com`: different host (subdomains count). - vs `https://app.example.com:8443`: different port. ### What SOP restricts - **Reading** cross-origin responses from `fetch`/XHR (unless CORS allows it). - **Accessing the DOM** of a cross-origin iframe or popup (`iframe.contentWindow.document`). - Reading cross-origin **storage**: `localStorage`, IndexedDB and cookies are scoped to their own origin (cookies use slightly different "site" rules). - Reading pixels from a cross-origin image drawn on a canvas (the canvas becomes "tainted"). ### What SOP allows - **Embedding**: ``, `

j101.q: How does the event loop work internally?
j101.a:
**Internally, the browser's event loop repeatedly picks one task from its task queues, runs it to completion, performs a microtask checkpoint (draining every microtask), and then, when a frame is due, runs the rendering steps; Node.js runs a different, phase-based loop built on libuv.**

### The browser loop, per the HTML spec
1. **Pick a task.** There are several task queues (user input, timers, networking, messaging). The browser may prioritise some, for example input over timers, but runs tasks from the same queue in order.
2. **Run it** on the call stack until the stack is empty.
3. **Microtask checkpoint**: run microtasks until the queue is empty, including ones added during this step (promise reactions, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`).
4. **Update the rendering** if a frame is due (roughly every 16.7 ms at 60 Hz, only for visible documents): run `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks, then style, layout and paint. `IntersectionObserver` and `ResizeObserver` callbacks also run around this step.
5. If there is spare time, run `requestIdleCallback` callbacks.

### Important consequences
- A `Promise.then` chain that keeps adding microtasks **starves** rendering and input.
- `requestAnimationFrame` is the right place for visual updates: it runs just before paint.
- `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is clamped to at least 4 ms after 5 nested levels, and heavily throttled in background tabs.
- Long tasks (over 50 ms) hurt INP (Interaction to Next Paint). Break work into chunks or move it to a Web Worker; `scheduler.postTask` and `scheduler.yield()` give finer control where supported.

### Node.js (libuv) phases
**timers** (`setTimeout`/`setInterval`) → **pending callbacks** → **poll** (I/O) → **check** (`setImmediate`) → **close callbacks**. Between each callback, Node drains `process.nextTick` callbacks first, then promise microtasks.

j102.a:
**Garbage collection is the engine's automatic memory management: it periodically finds objects that can no longer be reached from your program and frees their memory, so you never free memory manually in JavaScript.**

### Reachability
An object is kept alive if it can be reached from a **root**: the global object, the current call stack (local variables and arguments), and active closures, timers or event listeners. Anything not reachable is garbage, even if objects in a group still reference each other (cycles are collected too).

### How modern engines do it (V8 as an example)
- **Mark-and-sweep**: starting from the roots, mark everything reachable, then reclaim everything unmarked.
- **Generational collection**: most objects die young, so new objects go into a small "young generation" collected often and cheaply (a scavenger). Survivors are promoted to the "old generation", which is collected less often.
- **Incremental and concurrent marking**: work is split up and done partly on background threads to avoid long pauses that would cause jank.
- **Compaction**: moving objects together to reduce fragmentation.

### What you control
- Do not keep references you no longer need (remove listeners, clear timers, empty caches).
- Use `WeakMap`, `WeakSet` and `WeakRef` when you want to associate data with objects without keeping them alive.
- `FinalizationRegistry` lets you run cleanup after an object is collected, but timing is not guaranteed, so never rely on it for program logic.

### Observing it
Chrome DevTools' Memory panel (heap snapshots, allocation timelines) shows what is retained and why. `performance.memory` (Chrome-only) gives rough numbers.

j103.a:
**A memory leak is memory your program no longer needs but that cannot be freed, because something still references it; in JavaScript that means an unintended reference keeps objects reachable, so the garbage collector cannot reclaim them and memory grows over time.**

### Common causes in front-end code
- **Event listeners not removed**, especially on `window`/`document` from components that mount and unmount.
- **Timers and intervals** that are never cleared and capture large data in their closures.
- **Detached DOM nodes**: elements removed from the page but still referenced from JavaScript (in an array, a cache, or a closure).
- **Unbounded caches**: a `Map` or object used as a cache that only ever grows.
- **Subscriptions** (WebSocket handlers, observables, store subscriptions) without unsubscribe.
- **Accidental globals** (assigning to undeclared variables in sloppy mode).
- **Closures** holding on to big objects longer than intended.

### Symptoms
The page gets slower over time, memory in Task Manager keeps rising, and the app may eventually crash, especially in long-lived SPAs and dashboards.

### Prevention
- Clean up in the same place you set up: React's effect cleanup, `AbortController` signals for listeners, `clearInterval`, `unsubscribe()`.
- Bound your caches (LRU with a maximum size) or use `WeakMap` when keyed by objects.
- Avoid storing DOM nodes long-term; store ids and look nodes up when needed.

### Finding leaks
Chrome DevTools → Memory → take heap snapshots before and after repeating an action several times, compare them, and look for growing object counts and "Detached" DOM trees. The retainers view shows exactly what keeps an object alive.

j104.a:
**A `WeakMap` is a key-value collection whose keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols) and are held weakly: an entry does not stop its key from being garbage-collected, and once the key is gone the entry disappears automatically.**

### Differences from Map
| | `Map` | `WeakMap` |
|---|---|---|
| Keys | Any value | Objects (and non-registered symbols) only |
| Keeps keys alive | Yes | No |
| Iterable / `size` | Yes | No |
| Methods | `get`, `set`, `has`, `delete`, `clear`, iteration | `get`, `set`, `has`, `delete` |

It cannot be iterated or sized because its contents can change whenever the garbage collector runs.

### Use cases
- **Attaching data to objects you don't own** (DOM nodes, library objects) without modifying them and without causing leaks.
- **Caching results per object**: memoise computations keyed by an object; the cache entry dies with the object.
- **Private data** for classes (the pre-`#private` technique).
- Tracking which objects have already been processed.

### When to use something else
- Need to list or count entries, or use primitive keys: use `Map`.
- Just need to remember objects (no value): use `WeakSet`.
- Need to hold an object weakly and check later whether it is still alive: `WeakRef`.

j105.a:
**A `WeakSet` is a collection of objects held weakly: you can add, check and remove objects, but it does not keep them alive, cannot be iterated and has no size.**

### API
`add(obj)`, `has(obj)`, `delete(obj)`. Values must be objects (or non-registered symbols).

### Use cases
WeakSet answers one question: **"have I seen or marked this object?"**, without leaking memory.
- **Tracking processed objects**: avoid handling the same node or request twice.
- **Cycle detection** in recursive algorithms such as deep clone, deep equal or serialisation.
- **Branding**: mark instances created by your own factory or class so other code can verify them (`trusted.has(obj)`).
- **Flagging DOM elements** (initialised, observed) without adding properties to them.

### WeakSet vs Set
A `Set` keeps every member alive forever until you delete it, which is a leak if you only use it as a "seen" marker for short-lived objects. A `WeakSet` lets the garbage collector remove members automatically.

### Limits
You cannot list its contents or know its size, because members can disappear at any time. If you need that, use a `Set` and clean up yourself.

j106.a:
**`Symbol` is a primitive type whose values are always unique; symbols are mainly used as property keys that cannot collide with any other key, and well-known symbols let you customise how built-in language features treat your objects.**

### Creating symbols
- `Symbol("description")`: a new, unique symbol every time. The description is only a label for debugging.
- `Symbol.for("key")`: a **global registry** symbol; the same key returns the same symbol everywhere, even across realms such as iframes.

### Symbols as property keys
- Guaranteed not to clash with string keys or other libraries' keys.
- **Hidden from** `for...in`, `Object.keys`, and `JSON.stringify`. They are not private, though: `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` and `Reflect.ownKeys` reveal them. (For real privacy, use `#private` fields.)

### Well-known symbols
- **`Symbol.iterator`**: makes an object iterable with `for...of` and spread.
- **`Symbol.asyncIterator`**: for `for await...of`.
- **`Symbol.toPrimitive`**: control conversion to numbers and strings.
- **`Symbol.toStringTag`**: customise `Object.prototype.toString` output.
- **`Symbol.hasInstance`**: customise `instanceof`.
- **`Symbol.dispose` / `Symbol.asyncDispose`**: used by the `using` declarations from the explicit resource management proposal, which is rolling out in engines.

### Use cases
Library metadata that will not collide with user properties, enum-like constants that cannot be confused with strings, and implementing language protocols like iteration.

j107.a:
**`BigInt` is a numeric primitive for integers of any size, written with an `n` suffix (`123n`) or created with `BigInt(value)`; it exists because regular `number`s lose precision beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1).**

### Why it is needed
`number` is a 64-bit float and represents every integer exactly only up to 9,007,199,254,740,991. Beyond that, `9007199254740993` silently becomes `9007199254740992`. That breaks database ids (Twitter/X, Discord snowflakes), financial calculations in minor units, cryptography and high-precision timestamps.

### Rules
- **No mixing** with `number` in arithmetic: `1n + 1` throws a `TypeError`. Convert explicitly with `BigInt(x)` or `Number(big)` (which may lose precision).
- **Division truncates** towards zero: `7n / 2n === 3n`.
- Comparisons work across types: `1n < 2` is `true`, `1n == 1` is `true`, `1n === 1` is `false`.
- `Math` functions do not accept BigInt.
- `typeof 10n` is `"bigint"`.
- `JSON.stringify` **throws** on BigInt; convert to a string first (or define `BigInt.prototype.toJSON` in your app, carefully).
- No unary `+` (`+1n` throws).

### When to use it
- Large integer ids from APIs: keep them as strings in JSON, convert to BigInt only for arithmetic.
- Exact integer arithmetic beyond 2^53.

### When not to
Decimals (BigInt is integers only) and ordinary counters: BigInt is slower than `number`. For money, store integer cents (a `number` is fine up to large amounts) or use a decimal library.

j108.a:
**A `Proxy` wraps a target object and lets you intercept fundamental operations on it (reading, writing, deleting, checking, enumerating, calling) through handler functions called traps.**

### Syntax
`const proxy = new Proxy(target, handler)`. Any trap you do not define falls through to the target.

### Common traps
- `get(target, prop, receiver)`: property reads.
- `set(target, prop, value, receiver)`: writes; return `true` on success (returning `false` throws in strict mode).
- `has` (the `in` operator), `deleteProperty`, `ownKeys` (`Object.keys`, `for...in`), `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, `defineProperty`.
- `apply` and `construct` when the target is a function.

### Real-world uses
- **Reactivity**: Vue 3 and MobX track which properties a component reads and re-render when they change.
- **Validation** of writes (see "How to use Proxy for validation").
- **Default values** for missing properties, and negative array indexes.
- **Logging, tracing and access control** (read-only views, hiding private keys).
- **API clients** that build URLs from property access (`api.users.get()`).
- Mocks and test spies.

### Best practices
- Inside traps, use **`Reflect`** methods (`Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver)`) to perform the default behaviour correctly, including getters and inheritance.
- Respect **invariants**: for example, a non-configurable property must keep reporting its real value, or the engine throws.

### Costs and limits
Every intercepted operation runs your code, so proxies are slower than plain objects. Avoid them in very hot paths. Some built-ins with internal slots (`Map`, `Date`, private class fields) do not work transparently through a proxy without extra care.

j109.a:
**`Reflect` is a built-in object with static methods that perform the default behaviour of fundamental object operations (`get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `ownKeys`, `apply`, `construct`...), with the same names and arguments as Proxy traps.**

### Why it exists
1. **Companion to Proxy**: inside a trap, `Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver)` does exactly what the engine would have done, including getters and inheritance, so you can add behaviour and then forward cleanly.
2. **Better return values**: `Reflect.set` and `Reflect.defineProperty` return `true`/`false` instead of throwing or failing silently.
3. **Function form of operators**: `Reflect.has(obj, key)` instead of `key in obj`, and `Reflect.deleteProperty` instead of `delete`, which is handy for functional code.
4. **Complete key listing**: `Reflect.ownKeys(obj)` returns string **and** symbol keys, including non-enumerable ones.
5. **Safe function calls**: `Reflect.apply(fn, thisArg, args)` works even if `fn` has its own `apply` property.

### The receiver argument
`Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver)` passes `receiver` as `this` to getters. In a Proxy, forwarding the `receiver` ensures that getters reading other properties also go through the proxy, which matters for inheritance and reactivity.

### Reflect vs Object
Many methods overlap (`Object.getPrototypeOf` vs `Reflect.getPrototypeOf`). The `Reflect` versions are designed for meta-programming: consistent arguments and boolean results instead of exceptions.

### Reflect.construct
Calls a constructor with an arguments array and optionally a different `new.target`, useful when building factories or subclasses dynamically.

j110.a:
**A generic `curry(fn)` returns a function that collects arguments across calls and invokes the original function once it has received at least `fn.length` arguments; until then it returns another function waiting for the rest.**

### The algorithm
1. Read the target arity from `fn.length`.
2. Return a function `curried(...args)`.
3. If `args.length >= arity`, call `fn` with those arguments (keeping `this`).
4. Otherwise return a new function that, when called with more arguments, calls `curried` with the old and new arguments combined.

This version accepts several arguments per step, so `add(1)(2)(3)`, `add(1, 2)(3)` and `add(1)(2, 3)` all work. That is what libraries like Lodash and Ramda do.

### Edge cases to mention in an interview
- **`fn.length` ignores** rest parameters and parameters with defaults, so `curry((a, b = 2) => ...)` thinks the arity is 1. Allow an explicit arity: `curry(fn, arity)`.
- **Variadic functions** (like `sum(...nums)`) cannot be curried by length. A common variant collects until it is called with no arguments: `sum(1)(2)(3)()`.
- **Placeholders** (Lodash's `_`) let you skip arguments; an optional extension.
- Preserve `this` by using `apply`.

### Why it matters
Curried helpers make configuration-first functions (`log("error")(message)`), point-free pipelines, and reusable predicates (`hasRole("admin")`) easy to create.

j111.a:
**A pure function always returns the same output for the same inputs and has no side effects: it does not modify its arguments, external variables, the DOM, storage or the network, and does not depend on anything that can change between calls.**

### The two rules
1. **Deterministic**: same arguments, same result. No dependence on `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, global mutable state, or the current time and user.
2. **No side effects**: no mutating inputs, no writing to outer variables, no logging, no requests.

### Why they are valuable
- **Easy to test**: give inputs, assert outputs, no mocks or setup.
- **Easy to reason about**: the signature tells the whole story.
- **Safe to memoise and cache**, since results never change for the same input.
- **Safe to run in parallel, retry or reorder.**
- **Framework requirements**: React expects component rendering and state reducers to be pure (Strict Mode deliberately calls them twice to expose impurity), and Redux reducers must be pure.

### Turning impure into pure
- Pass the changing value in as an argument: `formatDate(date, now)` instead of reading `new Date()` inside.
- Return a new value instead of mutating: `[...list, item]` instead of `list.push(item)`.
- Keep side effects at the edges of the program (event handlers, effects, API layers) and keep the core logic pure ("functional core, imperative shell").

### Reality check
Programs need side effects to be useful. The goal is not zero side effects, but isolating them so most logic is pure.

j112.a:
**A side effect is anything a function does besides computing and returning a value: changing state outside itself, mutating its arguments, or interacting with the outside world such as the network, DOM, storage, timers or console.**

### Examples
- Mutating a parameter or a global/outer variable.
- Updating the DOM.
- HTTP requests, WebSocket messages.
- Reading or writing `localStorage`, cookies, files.
- Logging, analytics, `alert`.
- Starting timers, subscribing to events.
- Reading changing values like `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` (strictly, these make a function impure rather than being side effects themselves).

### Side effects are necessary
A program with no side effects cannot show anything or save anything. The goal is to **control** them:
- Keep core logic pure and push side effects to the boundaries (handlers, effects, services).
- Make them explicit and easy to find.
- Make them idempotent where possible (safe to repeat).
- Always pair setup with cleanup (unsubscribe, clear timers, abort requests).

### In React
Rendering must be pure. Side effects go in **event handlers** (in response to user actions) or **`useEffect`** (to synchronise with external systems), with cleanup functions. Fetching data is increasingly done in Server Components, route loaders or libraries like TanStack Query rather than raw effects.

### Testing
Functions with side effects need mocks or fakes for the outside world. Isolating effects behind small adapters keeps that manageable.

j113.a:
**Immutability patterns are techniques for updating data by creating new versions instead of mutating existing ones, such as spread updates, non-mutating array methods, structural sharing, freezing, and helper libraries like Immer.**

### Core patterns
- **Object update**: `{ ...obj, key: value }`.
- **Nested update**: copy each level along the changed path: `{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, address: { ...state.user.address, city } } }`.
- **Array add/remove/update**: `[...list, item]`, `list.filter(i => i.id !== id)`, `list.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i)`.
- **ES2023 copies**: `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, `with(index, value)`.
- **Remove a key**: `const { removed, ...rest } = obj`.
- **Maps/Sets**: create a new one: `new Map(old).set(k, v)`.

### Structural sharing
Only the changed path is copied; everything else is reused by reference. This keeps updates cheap and lets libraries detect changes with `===`, which is how React, Redux and memoisation decide what to re-render.

### Enforcing immutability
- `Object.freeze` (shallow) or a recursive deep freeze in development.
- TypeScript's `readonly` and `Readonly<T>`, `as const`.

### Immer
Write "mutating" code against a draft; Immer produces the immutable result with structural sharing. Redux Toolkit uses it internally. It shines with deeply nested state.

### Normalise deep state
If updates require copying five levels deep, flatten the data (store entities by id in maps) so updates touch one level.

j114.a:
**A higher-order function is a function that takes another function as an argument, returns a function, or both; it is possible because functions are values in JavaScript.**

### Built-in examples
`map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `forEach`, `sort`, `find`, `some`, `every`, `setTimeout`, `addEventListener`, `Promise.then`. They all take a function that defines the specific behaviour, while they handle the general part (looping, scheduling, waiting).

### Functions that return functions
- **Function factories**: `makeMultiplier(2)`.
- **Decorators/wrappers** that add behaviour to an existing function: `debounce`, `throttle`, `memoize`, `once`, logging, retry, timing.
- **Middleware**: Express and Redux middleware are functions returning functions.
- **Currying and partial application**.

### Why they matter
- **Abstraction**: separate *what* to do from *how* to iterate, wait or repeat.
- **Reuse**: one `retry` wrapper works for any async function.
- **Composition**: small functions combine into pipelines.
- **Declarative code**: `users.filter(isActive).map(toCard)` reads like a description of the result.

### In React
Hooks and render functions are built on the same idea. Higher-order components (`withAuth(Component)`) were the classic pattern before hooks; they still appear in older codebases.

### Tip
Keep the functions you pass in small and named (`isActive`, `byDate`) so higher-order calls read like sentences.

j115.a:
**Memoization is caching a function's results by its arguments, so repeated calls with the same inputs return the stored result instead of recomputing it; it trades memory for speed and only works for pure functions.**

### How it works
Wrap the function; on each call build a key from the arguments, return the cached value if present, otherwise compute, store and return it.

### Choosing the cache key
- Single primitive argument: use it directly as a `Map` key.
- Several primitives: join them or nest Maps.
